items.title: [Comment] Mitapivat in the RISE UP trial: a new therapy for sickle cell disease
items.summary: Sickle cell disease is the most common haemoglobinopathy, affecting more than 7 million people worldwide.1 Despite substantial morbidity and mortality, access to effective disease-modifying therapies remains limited.2,3 Hydroxyurea and chronic blood transfusions have both been shown to reduce acute sickle cell disease complications, including vaso-occlusive crises and stroke, while also improving haematological parameters.4,5 However, the availability and long-term feasibility of both could be limited in some settings.

items.title: [Comment] Offline: Berlin diary
items.summary: “WHO is a retirement home…We must reinvent multilateralism…We must be more candid with one another…We do not spend enough time talking with people who totally disagree with us…I have seen very few SDG badges…On trust, AI will not help…The paradox of using a product of science to disseminate anti-science…It's super-important we don't get infected by the negativity.” These were some of the reflections exchanged during a meeting, held under the Chatham House Rule, at last week's World Health Summit in Berlin.

items.title: [Perspectives] Wisdom and tenderness
items.summary: In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, the widespread mental health toll of the pandemic was quickly appreciated by communities, educators, and health-care providers. Children, adolescents, and young adults generally fared the worst, despite having lower rates of severe COVID-19 morbidity, hospitalisations, and death than older adults. And an additional widespread concern was uncovered that had predated the pandemic, but which pandemic restrictions brought forward in stark relief, that of loneliness.

items.title: [Perspectives] Longevity is a political concern
items.summary: Having immersed myself in death and dying for well over a decade—I wrote a book, The Way We Die Now (2016), and was later a member of the Lancet Commission on The Value of Death—it was inevitable that I would become interested in the flip side of that subject: the world of longevity. I use the word “world” because it has so many constituent parts: science, industry, economics, medicine, philosophy, religion, and politics.

items.summary: Many of the most potent antibiotics originate from bacteria. A large proportion belong to a class of compounds known as nonribosomal peptides (NRP). items.title: Scientists uncover the molecular pillars that shape our cells' powerpacks
items.summary: Mitochondria are the tiny powerpacks that supply most of the energy our cells need. Their ability to generate this energy relies on a distinctive architecture: two membranes, one tucked inside the other, separated by a narrow gap called the intermembrane space (IMS). This tiny space helps sustain the chemistry of energy production, making its organization critical to how these cellular powerpacks function.

items.title: As midterms loom, Trump and his allies try to change the subject

items.summary: During the Syrian war (2011–24), the Assad Government forces and their Russian allies conducted hundreds of strikes on medical facilities in opposition-held areas. Monitoring groups documented over 600 attacks on health care, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of health-care workers throughout the conflict. Hospitals in eastern Aleppo and other contested regions were reduced to rubble. Surgeons operated in underground rooms illuminated by generators, and ambulances were targeted while transporting patients between sites.

items.title: [Perspectives] Temporal rationing: a man with gastric cancer in Colombia
items.summary: Pepe, a 45-year-old man living in the city of Cali, Colombia, worked as a self-employed hauler of goods with a wheelbarrow. In 2010, he presented to a general practitioner with several months of abdominal heaviness and non-exertional substernal burning. The physician provisionally diagnosed gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and prescribed omeprazole. However, Pepe's symptoms slowly worsened and 10 weeks later he returned to the physician, who ordered a gastroscopy, which occurred 2 months later, revealing an ulcerated mass.
